# Introduction {-}
We are going to look at data about publication times for articles funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute. The data are from the `ISLR2` package, but are not used in [the text](#r2).

# Packages {-}

Loading the [standard packages](#r1) for this course:
```{r}
library(ISLR2) # package contains the data files
library(mbadtools, quietly=TRUE) # for mbad courses
```

# Data {-}
We get the data from the package. The data are from [Gordon et al., 2013](#r3).
```{r}
data(Publication)
?Publication
Publication
```

# Data Description {-}
An initial attempt at description uses `skim`.

```{r}
Publication %>% skim
```

There are 244 rows and 9 columns. There is one character variable, with 14 different values, not a candidate for a factor. 

A glimpse is always useful.
```{r}
Publication %>% glimpse
```

>Publication {ISLR2}	R Documentation

>Time-to-Publication Data

>Description Publication times for 244 clinical trials funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.

>Format A data frame with 244 observations, each representing a clinical trial, and 9 variables:

|Column | Description|
|-------|----------------------|
|posres|Did the trial produce a positive (significant) result? 1=Yes, 0=No.|
|multi|Did the trial involve multiple centers? 1=Yes, 0=No.|
|clinend|Did the trial focus on a clinical endpoint? 1=Yes, 0=No.|
|mech|Funding mechanism within National Institute of Health: a qualitative variable.|
|sampsize|Sample size for the trial.|
|budget|Budget of the trial, in millions of dollars.|
|impact|Impact of the trial; this is related to the number of publications.|
|time|Time to publication, in months.|
|status|Whether or not the trial was published at time: 1=Published, 0=Not yet published.|

# Data Wrangling {-}

Four columns seem to be a 0-1 variable. Let's make them factors. This is optional, but we don't want regression to treat them as meaningful numeric values.

```{r}
Publication1 = Publication %>%
  mutate(across(c(posres, multi, clinend, status),
                factor) )
Publication1 %>% skim
```
This did the job.

# Data Visualization
A `ggpairs` plot of the numeric variables is a good idea.
```{r fig.height=12, fig.width=12}
Publication1 %>% select(where(is.numeric)) %>% ggpairs(progress=F)
```

Most papers were published fast, but there aren't any other readily observable patterns.

# Research Problem {-}

We will see whether `sampsize`, `budget` and `impact` have an influence on publication time.  Perhaps a linear model applies.

# Analysis {-}
We will try a linear model.

```{r message=FALSE}
linfit = lm(time ~ sampsize + budget + impact, data=Publication1)
linfit %>% glance %>% gt_add_significance()
linfit %>% tidy(conf.int=TRUE) %>% gt_add_significance()
```

The tidy shows us that `sampsize` and `budget` are not significant, their coefficients might well be zero. But `impact` has a negative relation to time. The adjusted R-squared is only .12, or 12% of the variation explained by this model. Not much.

## Residual analysis
We make some graphs of the residuals for analysis.

```{r message=FALSE}
linfit %>% gg_residual_plots()
```

There is an upward rise in the QQ plot, signifying that the residuals are not normally distributed. The Resid plot does show a mean of about 0, but there is significant variation in the larger fitted values compared to the smaller ones, a possible violation of assumptions. Finally in the LS plot there is rising variation with fitted values, not supporting the assumption of homoscedasticity.

We are not happy with this model.

# Including factors
We extend the analysis by adding `posres`,`multi`, and `clinend` factor variables. A positive result, more than one center, or a clinical end might influence the time to publication.

```{r}
linfit2 = lm(
  time ~ sampsize + budget + impact + posres + multi + clinend,
  data=Publication1)
linfit2 %>% glance %>% gt_add_significance()
linfit2 %>% tidy(conf.int=TRUE) %>% gt_add_significance()
```

The `glance` shows that the adjusted r-squared did not go up. The `tidy` shows that none of the new variables have coefficients significantly different from zero. In fact, again only `impact` is significant.

## Residuals 2
I do not think this will be better.
```{r}
linfit2 %>% gg_residual_plots()
```

And indeed it is not.

# Baseline with impact only

We will analyze the regression with only `impact` before looking at other models. 

```{r}
linfit1 = lm(time ~ impact, data=Publication1)
linfit1 %>% glance %>% gt_add_significance()
linfit1 %>% tidy(conf.int=TRUE) %>% gt_add_significance()
```

The adjusted r-squared does not change, around .12. But at least there are fewer variables. The impact is significant, and negative, as we might expect--- high-impact journals might tke longer in th review process. We will check residuals.
```{r}
linfit1 %>% gg_residual_plots()
```

No worse and no better.

Occam's Razor tells us that the last regression model, `linfit1`, is best so far, being easier to explain.

# Does status matter?

Maybe the status of the article makes a difference in the time, as well as the impact.

```{r}
linfits = lm(time ~ impact + status, data=Publication1)
linfits %>% glance %>% gt_add_significance()
linfits %>% tidy(conf.int=TRUE) %>% gt_add_significance()
linfits  %>% gg_residual_plots()
```

`status` does not seem to matter, as its coefficient might as well be zero.

# Funding Mechanism

There's one more variable, `mech`, that we have not tried yet. It has 14 discrete values, which cannot be handled properly as a factor.

Let's explore by looking at the distribution of data.

```{r fig.height=12, fig.width=12}
Publication1 %>% ggplot() +
  geom_boxplot(aes(mech, time, color=mech), show.legend=F)+
  theme_bw()
```

Funding mechanism R01 seems to yield some very long pub times, with U04 a distant second. But the medians are all in a similar range. Contract mechanism seems to deliver shortest median pub times. U54 seems to have only a few entries.

# Impact and `posres`
You would think that a positive result and impact taken together would make a bigger difference than one or the other. This is called an interaction effect.  That's a conjecture, framed as a hypothesis. Let's test it.

```{r}
linfiti = lm(time ~ impact*posres, data=Publication1)
linfiti %>% glance %>% gt_add_significance()
linfiti %>% tidy(conf.int=TRUE) %>% gt_add_significance()
linfiti %>% gg_residual_plots()
```

Neither `posres` nor the product of `posres` and `impact` makes any difference; both coefficients are not significantly different from zero. The r-squared doesn't change. 

Residuals behavior is not improved.

# Conclusion {-}
My conclusions are that the simplest model with only `impact` as a driver is the best of a bad lot.  None of them has much predictive value. 

Perhaps publication times of results are not influenced much, if at all, by any of these drivers.  It's mostly random.

We also saw how to make a table in the text. Kind of funky, but doable.
